body:
For background the `inherits` descriptor was made mandatory because the obviously reasonable default value, is also more expensive so @tabatkins felt it should always be a conscious decision.
FWIW I agree that it should have been optional — it's an antipattern when transient performance considerations drive API design. But hey, at least we can always _make_ it optional!

I also think we _could_ have reasonable initial initial values (yes, I just did that 😅) for the `initial-value` descriptor instead of requiring it every time. `0px`, `transparent`, `image(transparent)` etc. 

And yes, `syntax: "*"` should just be the default.

@Crissov You're mixing two things here, which I think should be discussed separately:

1. Allowing to overwrite and extend an existing custom property definition. (Currently [the last one wins](https://drafts.css-houdini.org/css-properties-values-api-1/#at-ruledef-property:~:text=the%20last%20one%20in%20stylesheet%20order%20%22wins%22%2E).)
2. Making all descriptors optional.

So I suggest to open a separate issue to discuss point 1.

Regarding point 2, it also tripped me up many times that the `inherits` descriptor is not optional. So yes, I'm also for making them optional.

> For background the `inherits` descriptor was made mandatory because the obviously reasonable default value, is also more expensive so @tabatkins felt it should always be a conscious decision.

What is the obvious reasonable default value? For me, it would be _not_ to inherit, as most of the properties I define don't need to inherit. (And yes, that goes against how unregistered properties behave, so against what @AtkinsSJ [wrote](https://github.com/w3c/csswg-drafts/issues/13211#issuecomment-3646867827).) But I get the point that it would be more consistent to let them inherit by default.

Either way, I don't get the argument why that should be more expensive. If it's to inherit by default, then it's not different to declaring them via declarations, which is what authors usually do. And _not_ inheriting by default sounds less expensive to me.
So maybe you or @tabatkins could provide some background here?

Sebastian

@AtkinsSJ 

> Perhaps the default values should match how an unregistered custom property behaves? Or at least as close as possible. 

Yup. That’s on par with the [principle of least surprise](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Principle_of_least_astonishment): you declare the things that are different from the default behavior, rather than having a bunch of things change that you did not declare, requiring you to write extra code to go back to the default behavior.

> `initial-value` is the only part that's tricky there I think as it would be the `<guaranteed-invalid-value>` which isn't representable, though it is already the default if it's not specified.
> 
> So these would be equivalent:
> 
> @property --a {};
> 
> @property --a {
> 	inherits: true;
> 	syntax: "*";
> 	/* initial-value: guaranteed-invalid-value; */
> };

Ooh I really, _really_ like this.  Currently there is no way to register a custom property and still have fallbacks, which limits what you can do with it. This would solve that AND the ergonomics issue in one fell swoop.

----


@SebastianZ 
> What is the obvious reasonable default value? For me, it would be _not_ to inherit, as most of the properties I define don't need to inherit. (And yes, that goes against how unregistered properties behave, so against what [@AtkinsSJ](https://github.com/AtkinsSJ) [wrote](https://github.com/w3c/csswg-drafts/issues/13211#issuecomment-3646867827).) But I get the point that it would be more consistent to let them inherit by default.

See above.

Also I would question how universal this is:
> For me, it would be _not_ to inherit, as most of the properties I define don't need to inherit.

This has not been my experience, at all. Most of the properties I define _do_ need to inherit.

> Either way, I don't get the argument why that should be more expensive. If it's to inherit by default, then it's not different to declaring them via declarations, which is what authors usually do. And _not_ inheriting by default sounds less expensive to me. So maybe you or [@tabatkins](https://github.com/tabatkins) could provide some background here?

IIRC inheriting was more expensive. I agree it's no different to declaring them via declarations. Perhaps @tabatkins can clarify.

My reason for combining both topics in one issue is that I’d be fine with requiring some or all descriptors to be set explicitly for the _final_ registration of a custom property to take effect, but I believe that in each individual ruleset every declaration should be optional. It follows naturally that later definitions only overwrite the values of descriptors they set explicitly.
I'm fine with making descriptors optional. I'm not convinced about cascading the descriptors independently like declarations in style rules. AFAIK all at-rules are atomic.

Agenda+ to get resolutions on the following:
1. Do we have consensus to make `inherits` optional?
	1. If so, what should be the default value?
2. Do we have consensus to make `initial-value` optional?
	1. If so, what should be the default value? 

IMO: The model should be "behave like an unregistered property in every way except those declared". Then, the initial values fall out of that very naturally:
- `true` for `inherits`
- Guaranteed invalid for `initial-value` (proposed by @AtkinsSJ). I like this a lot better than my own idea around recursively generating a reasonable initial value.

> If so, what should be the default value? (Guaranteed invalid seems the best proposal so far)

Guaranteed invalid is probably the easiest choice. But it could be more useful for authors if we pick the initial value depending on the syntax, e.g.

 - `*` and `<custom-ident>` default to guaranteed invalid
 - `<number>` and `<integer>` default to `0`
 - Dimensions default to have a numerical value of zero. The unit shouldn't matter, but could pick the canonical one if needed. E.g. `<length>` would default to `0px`.
 - `<percentage>` defaults to `0%`
 - `<length-percentage>` defaults to `0px`
 - `<string>` defaults to `""`
 - `<color>` defaults to `transparent`. Or maybe solid `black`?
 - `<url>` and `<image>` default to `url()`
 - `<transform-function>` defaults to `scale(1)` or similar
 - If there is a `|` combinator, default to the left hand side
 - If there is a `+` or `#` multiplier, the default is a list of 1 item

@Loirooriol That was exactly what I was thinking at first, but guaranteed invalid is actually *more* useful for authors, because **they can provide fallbacks that are different per use**. This is a big limitation of the existing `@property` syntax, that fallbacks are global. So, by doing it that way, not only we help ergonomics, we actually plug a gap too. So I'm currently quite strongly in favor of this direction.

I don't think "valid" default values are at all reasonable as a general case here, yeah. Like, there's *no way* for us to know that an empty string is a reasonable default for a `<string>` value. Numerics are *usually* 0, but definitely not always. etc.

Defaulting *all* the descriptors to what an unregistered normal property does seems like the right thing to me. Syntax of `*`, initial value of guaranteed-invalid, inherits of `true`. That's both simple (good) and I think gives reasonably useful behavior in all provide/omit possibilities.

And yeah, I've hit the issue *while writing `@function`'s spec* that it's a little annoying a custom property registration with a type can't still default to guaranteed-invalid; I didn't realize while first defining it that that would be useful, but it definitely is. In the spec I can just *say* that the registration has that initial value (and note that it's not something authors can do), but it would be useful to make it real.

Not being able to create guaranteed invalid values with registered custom props is also why it is impossible to create a transpiler for `@function`. So definitely would have been useful to have this, I suspect it will still be useful in the future.

The CSS Working Group just discussed ``[css-properties-values-api] `@property` descriptors should be optional whenever possible``, and agreed to the following: * `RESOLVED: make all property descriptors in @property optional`
The full IRC log of that discussion <ydaniv> TabAtkins: for now, for reasons we designed in the past, the @property does not give optional default values, all needs to be specified
<ydaniv> ... it proved to be annoyance in practice
<ydaniv> ... it's also been annoying in spec writing
<ydaniv> ... proposal is to make all descriptors in the @property optional as if it was untyped
<kizu> +calc(infinity) to the proposal
<ydaniv> ... I saw nothing but support on the thread
<ydaniv> +1
<miriam> +1 strong support
<kbabbitt> +1, this will also make writing supports-conditions for these easier

<ydaniv> PROPOSED RESOLUTION: make all property descriptors in @property optional
<astearns> ack emilio
<ydaniv> astearns: objections?

<astearns> ack kizu

<emilio> q-

Edits have been pushed in <https://github.com/w3c/css-houdini-drafts/commit/e1f11c5e6fffef319bcdc0f0fe25034d1a6a4b3f>

One tiny change that wasn't necessarily implied by this is that, previously, if you specify 'syntax' and 'initial-value', but 'initial-value' fails to parse according to the syntax, it would make the entire rule invalid. This was a side-effect of the fact that, if you had a 'syntax', an initial-value was *required*; we couldn't just drop the declaration.

But now we can; an omitted 'initial-value' sets it to the guarnateed-invalid value. So, I've changed the behavior here; if your initial-value fails to parse, just the declaration is dropped, so you'll get the GIV (or fall back to the previously-specified one, like normal for CSS fallback). This shouldn't be too observable.

[w3c/css-houdini-drafts@e1f11c5](https://github.com/w3c/css-houdini-drafts/commit/e1f11c5e6fffef319bcdc0f0fe25034d1a6a4b3f) removed the requirement of the `@property/initial-value` to be computationally independent when the `@property/syntax` is not `*`, when declared in CSS. But it still applies when declared with [`CSS.registerProperty()`](https://drafts.css-houdini.org/css-properties-values-api/#the-registerproperty-function):

  > If `parsed initial value` is not computationally independent, throw a `SyntaxError` and exit this algorithm.

Is it intentional?

(edit)

Moreover, it also changed the requirement on the initial value in `CSS.registerProperty()`.

Before, it was required to be computationally independent only if the syntax was not the universal syntax. 

  > Otherwise, if `syntax definition` is the universal syntax definition, parse `initialValue` according to `<declaration-value>?`.
  >
  > If this fails, throw a `SyntaxError` and exit this algorithm.
  >
  > Otherwise, let `parsed initial value` be the parsed result. **Skip to the next step of this algorithm.**

Now this requirement applies regardless of the syntax.

  > - parse `initialValue` according to `<declaration-value>?` if `syntax definition` is the universal syntax definition, and according to `syntax definition` otherwise.
  > - If parsing returns failure, throw a `SyntaxError` and exit this algorithm. Otherwise, let `parsed initial value` be the parsed result.
  > - If `parsed initial value` is not computationally independent, throw a `SyntaxError` and exit this algorithm.

I am not sure that what follows is worth opening separate issues, and if this has not already been raised elsewhere.

(1) Authors can write `@property --name {}`, `@layer name {}`, `@layer name;`, but not `@property --name;`. Should it be defined?

(2) Serializing `@property` is currently defined to include all descriptors except `initial-value` if omitted. Now that they are all optional, should they still be?
